# The Character of the Light

The first bird Marit Selby found on Skarra was a goldcrest, and it weighed five point four grams. She knew because she weighed it, on the little brass scale the Trust had left in the warden's hut along with a ruler, a ledger, a box of plastic bags, and a laminated sheet that said, in capitals, DO NOT HANDLE GULLS.

It was lying at the foot of the lighthouse on her first morning, on the concrete apron where the rainwater ran off the tower. Olive-green, no bigger than her thumb, with a stripe of gold along the crown as if applied with a fine brush. Its eyes were closed. She had seen enough closed eyes in her working life to know there was no point waiting for them to open, but she held it in her palm for a minute anyway, because that was also something she had learned.

Then she weighed it and measured its wing and wrote it in the ledger. *1 Sept. Goldcrest. 5.4g. Wing 54mm. Base of tower, NE side.* She bagged it and put it in the chest freezer, where someone from the university would collect it at the end of the season.

The advertisement had said: *Seasonal Warden, Skarra. September to November. Must be comfortable with solitude and with dead things.* Marit had read it twice in the library in town, a year after she'd retired from the hospice, and thought: well. That's me described.

---

Skarra was a mile long and half a mile wide at its fattest, a whaleback of turf and rock with the lighthouse at its northern end. The light had been automated in 1998. The keepers' cottages were still there, a low white terrace behind the tower, and the Trust kept one of them habitable for its warden: a bed, a stove, a wind-up radio, a shelf of field guides with other people's notes in the margins. The rest were shut up. Through their windows you could see wallpaper from the 1970s and a calendar from a year that had not known it would be the last.

The light itself needed nobody. A photocell on the gallery rail told it when dusk had come, and it came on, and the great lens began to turn on its bearing with a sound like someone breathing in through their teeth. Three white flashes, then darkness. Three white flashes. Every twenty seconds, all night, until the photocell saw the sun and told it to stop.

Marit's job was not the light. Her job was what the light did.

In September it did very little. The nights were clear, and the birds passing over Skarra steered by the stars and the turn of the earth and whatever else it was that birds knew, and they did not come down. Sometimes she could hear them, high up, the thin *tseep* of redwings going over in the dark. Some mornings there was nothing at the foot of the tower at all. Some mornings there was a wheatear, or a meadow pipit, or once a willow warbler so perfect it looked as though it had been set there on purpose. She walked the apron, then the gallery, then the rocks below the cliff, and wrote down what she found.

On quiet days she wrote emails on the Trust's satellite laptop, which worked for twenty minutes a day if she held it at a particular angle on the windowsill. Most of them were to the Lights Commission.

She had read the old reports before she came. She knew what happened on Skarra on certain nights in autumn, when the wind went round to the south-east and brought thick weather off the continent, and the cloud came down low, and there was a fine rain. On those nights the birds lost the stars. And the beam, which on a clear night was only a beam, turned solid in the wet air, a great white spoke wheeling through the dark, and the birds came to it. Nobody was entirely sure why. They circled it and circled it, in their hundreds, in their thousands, and some struck the glass, and some simply flew until there was nothing left in them and dropped. In October 1911 the keepers on Skarra had recorded fourteen hundred dead in a single night. Nobody had asked them to record it. They had done it anyway.

There were things that could be done. Other lights, elsewhere, had been dimmed on such nights, or had their towers floodlit so the birds could see the shape of what they were circling and land on it instead of hitting it. Marit sent the Commission the papers. She sent them the 1911 log, photographed page by page. She was polite, and then she was specific, and then she was polite again.

The Commission's replies were also polite. The light at Skarra, they wrote, was an aid to navigation maintained under statutory obligation. Its *character*, which was the word they used, could not be altered without a Notice to Mariners and a period of consultation. They thanked her for her interest.

---

The man who came to service the light was called Callum Reid. He came on the first Tuesday of each month in a rigid inflatable, with a toolbag and a flask. He was perhaps forty, with a beard going grey at the chin and the patient manner of someone who spends a lot of his life waiting for weather.

"You're the one sending the emails," he said, the first time, at the door of the tower.

"I am."

"They forward them to me." He didn't seem annoyed. "I don't know what they think I'm going to do about it."

She showed him the freezer. He looked in at the bags with their careful labels, the pipits and the warblers and a single song thrush with its speckled breast, and was quiet for a while.

"I didn't know it was that many," he said.

"That isn't many," said Marit. "That's September."

Afterwards she stood with him on the gallery while he drank his tea. From up there you could see the whole of Skarra, and the sea in every direction, and on the eastern horizon a container ship stacked like a child's blocks, going north.

"Does it need this?" she asked. "That ship. Does it need the light?"

Callum considered it. "No. He's got GPS, he's got radar, he's got a chart on a screen that knows every rock in the sea to the metre. He probably doesn't even look."

"Then what's it for?"

"For when all that goes." He screwed the cup back onto his flask. "Power fails. Satellite drops out. Somebody's in a wee boat with a phone that's died. It's the last thing. You don't take away the last thing because the other things usually work."

She didn't answer, and he seemed to take that as fair.

"You know why they call it the character?" he said, before he left. "Every light on this coast flashes different. Three every twenty seconds, that's Skarra. Two every fifteen is the Ness. Long-short is Haaf Point. So if you're out there and you see a light, you don't just know there's land. You count, and you know *which* land. You know where you are." He shrugged. "It's not just a light. It's a name."

---

In October the weather turned.

She heard it first on the shipping forecast, the calm voice going round the sea areas like a nurse on a ward round. *South-easterly four or five, increasing six later. Rain then drizzle. Moderate or poor, occasionally very poor.* She stood in the cottage kitchen with the kettle in her hand and listened to it twice.

Callum came out that afternoon, a week early, because a fault had shown on the monitoring system on the mainland: a sensor in the rotation reading wrong. He fixed it in two hours. By then the sea in the sound had got up, grey and short and slapping. He stood on the landing stage looking at it, then at the sky, then came back up the path.

"I'm not crossing in that," he said. "Is there a bed?"

There was a bed in the next cottage, under the 1970s wallpaper. She found him blankets. She made soup. They ate it at her table with the radio on, and at twenty past six the light came on outside the window without either of them touching anything, and the first flash went out across the drizzle like a held breath let go.

By eight the birds had come.

She heard them before she saw them. It was a sound she had read about and not been able to imagine: a thin continuous calling from every direction at once, hundreds of voices, *tseep* and *tsip* and the chack of fieldfares and something lower she didn't know. She put on her waterproofs and her head torch and went out, and Callum came after her.

From the foot of the tower the beam was a solid thing. It swung out of the lantern and away over the sea and came round again, and every time the birds were in it. They were like snow. They were like sparks off a fire, except that they did not rise. They turned with the light and followed it round, caught in it the way leaves are caught in a gutter. Thrushes. Starlings. Tiny pale flickers that must have been goldcrests. When the beam swung away they vanished, and the calling went on in the dark, and then the light came round and there they were again.

Something hit the glass above them with a sound like a knuckle on a door. Then another.

"Christ," said Callum quietly.

Something landed at Marit's feet. A redwing; she knew it by the cream stripe over the eye and the rust on its flank. It was alive. It sat on the wet concrete with its feathers puffed and its beak open, panting, and when she knelt and closed her hands round it, it did not try to move.

---

The control panel for the light was in a steel cabinet at the foot of the tower stair. Callum had shown it to her that afternoon as he packed his tools: a row of breakers, a status screen, a key switch marked LOCAL / REMOTE. On LOCAL there was a button for the lamp, so that a technician could work in the lantern without being blinded.

At half past nine Marit stood in front of it with the redwing inside her jacket, against her jumper, where it was warm.

She didn't hear Callum come in behind her. She only knew he was there when he said, "If you do that, they'll know within a minute. It alarms on the mainland."

"I know."

"They can't get anyone out tonight, but they'll put it on the radio. Navigational warning, Skarra light unlit." He paused. "And they'll take the job off you. Me too, probably, for showing you the key."

"I know," she said again.

She did not turn round. Through the small window in the tower door she could see the edge of the beam, sweeping, and the bright fleck of a bird in it, and another.

She thought about the nights on the ward. She thought about the machines that told you how a person was doing, that beeped and alarmed and lit up, that you could not switch off however much you wanted to on the nights when what they told you was hard. You didn't switch them off, because they were not there for you. They were there for whoever came after you, the next shift, the doctor who hadn't seen what you'd seen. What you switched off was your own wanting. You stayed, and you did what you could inside the light.

And then, out past the window, low on the horizon, she saw a ship.

Only its lights: a white masthead, a green to starboard. It was small and a long way off, moving steadily north through the murk. A fishing boat, maybe, or a coaster. Someone on a bridge with a mug of tea and a screen and the drizzle on the windows. Almost certainly they were fine. Almost certainly they had every instrument Callum had listed and did not need, had never needed, Skarra.

Almost certainly.

She thought: *I don't know who is on it.*

She took her hand off the key.

"Right," she said, and her voice came out steadier than she'd expected. "Then I'll need boxes."

---

They used everything. The cardboard boxes the Trust's supplies had come in. The cloth bags meant for the dead birds, which had never held live ones. A laundry basket from the empty cottage, with a towel over it. Her own rucksack, emptied onto the floor. They lined them with newspaper and set them in the oil store at the foot of the tower. It had no windows and was perfectly dark, and in the dark the birds would be still.

Then they went up.

The gallery was a narrow iron walkway around the outside of the lantern, with a rail at waist height. On an ordinary night it was just a place to stand. Tonight, when Marit came out of the little door into the wind, the rail was lined with birds. They clung to it all the way round, wet and puffed and blinking each time the beam swept over them. Thrushes and starlings and robins sat side by side, with a blackcap, a brambling with orange shoulders, and goldcrests in twos and threes pressed together like something knitted. More gripped the iron framework between the panes. More sat on the gallery floor. Every few seconds another came out of the dark and struck the glass and fell, or didn't fall, and held on.

The light behind the glass was almost unbearable. Each flash came round like a blow. She learned to turn her face from it and to work in its rhythm: three flashes, look, reach; darkness, cup your hands; three flashes, look again.

They took the birds off the rail one at a time. Most did not resist. A few were too far gone. She could feel it in the weight, or the lack of it, and in the way the head lolled, and those she put gently in her left pocket, for the ledger. The rest went into the bags, and when the bags were full Callum carried them down the hundred and eight steps to the oil store and came back up with them empty.

She lost track of time. She lost track of her hands, which went numb, and her face, which stung with rain. At some point she realised she was talking to the birds the way she used to talk to patients who could no longer hear her, a low steady nonsense: *There you are. There you are now. I've got you. That's it.* At some point she realised Callum was doing the same.

Around two in the morning a woodcock came down onto the gallery floor. It was a round bird the colour of dead bracken, with a long bill and enormous dark eyes set high on its head. It sat at her feet and looked up at her, or seemed to. She had never seen one so close. When she picked it up it was heavier than she'd expected, and warm, and its heart under her fingers was going like a small engine.

"Where've you come from?" she said. "Where've you come from, then?"

Norway, probably. Or further. It had crossed all that black water, in the rain, without stars, looking for something to tell it where it was. And it had found this.

She held it a moment longer than she needed to, in the dark between the flashes. Then she carried it down to the laundry basket herself, and climbed back up to the rail.

---

The drizzle stopped a little before five. She felt it before she saw it: a lightness in the air, the wind backing round. Overhead a single star came out, then a scattering of them, and the beam went thin and clear again. It was just light now, not a solid thing at all.

The calling changed. She could hear it lifting and drawing away to the south-west as the birds still flying found the sky again and followed it. Within half an hour the rail was nearly empty.

At ten to eight the photocell saw the dawn, and the light went out. The lens turned once more on its own momentum and was still.

They carried the boxes out onto the turf behind the cottages, inside the old drystone walls of the keepers' gardens, and opened them one by one.

Some birds went at once, bursting out of the box like something spilled upward, and were gone over the wall. Some sat blinking at the grey light, and then went. A few did not go at all, and Marit lifted them out and set them on the wall out of the wind, and most of those went after a while. The thrushes dropped into the long grass and almost immediately began to feed. The goldcrests went into the fuchsia that some keeper's wife had planted a hundred years ago, and could be heard in there ticking and whispering, like a clock being wound.

The woodcock was last. She tipped the laundry basket gently on its side and it walked out onto the grass as if it had all the time in the world. It looked around. Then it rose with a clatter of wings and went low and fast across the island and was gone.

Callum stood beside her with his hands in his pockets. His eyes were red. So, she supposed, were hers.

"How many?" he asked.

"I don't know yet." She had kept a tally on the back of her hand in biro until the rain took it. "I'll count."

---

He left at ten, when the sound had settled. At the landing stage he sat for a moment in the inflatable with his hand on the tiller.

"I'll write it up," he said. "What it looked like. It'll go in my report." He looked up at the tower. "Might be worth something, coming from me."

"Thank you," said Marit.

She watched him until he was a white wake and then nothing. Then she went up to the warden's hut and took out the ledger.

It took her the rest of the day. She weighed and measured every one of the dead: the ones from her pocket, and the ones from the apron and the rocks below. There were a hundred and sixty-three of them, laid out on the bench in rows. Redwings, mostly. Goldcrests. Starlings, robins, a single brambling. She held each one before she wrote it down.

Then she ruled a line down the middle of a fresh page and wrote, at the head of the second column, a word the ledger had never needed before. Underneath it she put her best count from the boxes and the bags and the basket. She wrote it with a question mark after it, because she was an honest woman and it had been a long night. It was more than four hundred.

At twenty past six she heard the lens begin to turn, that breath in through the teeth, and she went to the window. Out across the water the first flash went out. Then the second. Then the third. Then darkness, and the long count of twenty.

The sky was clear tonight. The birds would have their stars. But somewhere out there, she thought, someone might be looking at the dark and counting, needing to know where they were.

*Skarra*, the light said. *Skarra. Skarra.*

She would be up at dawn to see what it had cost.

---

*About 3,300 words, slightly over the 3,000 you asked for.*

The drizzle stopped a little before five. She felt it before she saw it: a lightness in the air, the wind backing round. Overhead a single star came out, then a scattering of them, and the beam went thin and clear again. It was just light now, not a solid thing at all.

The calling changed. She could hear it lifting and drawing away to the south-west as the birds still flying found the sky again and followed it. Within half an hour the rail was nearly empty.

At ten to eight the photocell saw the dawn, and the light went out. The lens turned once more on its own momentum and was still.

They carried the boxes out onto the turf behind the cottages, inside the old drystone walls of the keepers' gardens, and opened them one by one.

Some birds went at once, bursting out of the box like something spilled upward, and were gone over the wall. Some sat blinking at the grey light, and then went. A few did not go at all, and Marit lifted them out and set them on the wall out of the wind, and most of those went after a while. The thrushes dropped into the long grass and almost immediately began to feed. The goldcrests went into the fuchsia that some keeper's wife had planted a hundred years ago, and could be heard in there ticking and whispering, like a clock being wound.

The woodcock was last. She tipped the laundry basket gently on its side and it walked out onto the grass as if it had all the time in the world. It looked around. Then it rose with a clatter of wings and went low and fast across the island and was gone.

Callum stood beside her with his hands in his pockets. His eyes were red. So, she supposed, were hers.

"How many?" he asked.

"I don't know yet." She had kept a tally on the back of her hand in biro until the rain took it. "I'll count."

---

He left at ten, when the sound had settled. At the landing stage he sat for a moment in the inflatable with his hand on the tiller.

"I'll write it up," he said. "What it looked like. It'll go in my report." He looked up at the tower. "Might be worth something, coming from me."

"Thank you," said Marit.

She watched him until he was a white wake and then nothing. Then she went up to the warden's hut and took out the ledger.

It took her the rest of the day. She weighed and measured every one of the dead: the ones from her pocket, and the ones from the apron and the rocks below. There were a hundred and sixty-three of them, laid out on the bench in rows. Redwings, mostly. Goldcrests. Starlings, robins, a single brambling. She held each one before she wrote it down.

Then she ruled a line down the middle of a fresh page and wrote, at the head of the second column, a word the ledger had never needed before. Underneath it she put her best count from the boxes and the bags and the basket. She wrote it with a question mark after it, because she was an honest woman and it had been a long night. It was more than four hundred.

At twenty past six she heard the lens begin to turn, that breath in through the teeth, and she went to the window. Out across the water the first flash went out. Then the second. Then the third. Then darkness, and the long count of twenty.

The sky was clear tonight. The birds would have their stars. But somewhere out there, she thought, someone might be looking at the dark and counting, needing to know where they were.

*Skarra*, the light said. *Skarra. Skarra.*

She would be up at dawn to see what it had cost.
